notes: Opened to the public in 1876 as the New Delavan House. Andreas describes a 100-by-150-foot building, four hotel stories, about 50 rooms and capacity of 100; construction date remains unknown.

canonical_name: Carson, Pirie & Company North Division store opening
address_historical: 166-170 North Clark Street
structural_system: existing commercial building; material not stated
postfire_code_context: No physical construction is documented; this is a commercial occupancy event within the post-fire North Division.
notes: Andreas states that Carson, Pirie & Company opened a large dry-goods house at 166-170 North Clark in 1876. Building construction date and modification scope were not found.

canonical_name: Lincoln Park Floating Hospital pier and shelter use
address_historical: Lincoln Park lakefront north of North Avenue

structural_system: wooden pier with shelter house, railings, hammocks and cots
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Existing Lincoln Park pier
postfire_code_context: The wooden waterfront installation had a specialized park and pier use; ordinary city building-code applicability is uncertain.
notes: The Association received use of the roughly 400-foot pier in 1876 for a floating-hospital program. Andreas describes a shelter house and care equipment, but does not unambiguously date the shelter's erection; no construction completion is claimed.

canonical_name: West Side Water Works engine commissioning
address_historical: Twenty-second Street and Ashland Avenue
architect_or_builder: Quintard Iron Works (engines); City public works designers
structural_system: brick pumping station with stone trim; two compound condensing beam engines
postfire_code_context: Expanded pumping capacity was a central post-fire public-health and fire-protection investment.
notes: Engines entered operation November 6, 1876; formal specification tests in January 1877 measured 16,160,470 and 15,571,970 gallons per 24 hours and duties above 96 million foot-pounds. Included for the distinct 1877 commissioning/acceptance event, not as a 1877 building completion.

address_historical: Wabash Avenue near Monroe Street
structural_system: Illinois stone with brick trim; Victorian Gothic and Italianate masonry
postfire_code_context: Substantial masonry commercial construction within the expanded post-fire limits.
notes: Contemporary notices describe a five-story-and-basement, 40-by-155-foot, $30,000 store under construction in August-September 1877. Later facade, pediment, storefront, and finish alterations occurred; the building survives as the southern component of the landmark Haskell-Barker-Atwater group.

address_historical: Northwest corner of Ontario and Dearborn Streets
architect_or_builder: F. M. Whitehouse with Burling & Adler; John McEwen (contractor)
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Chicago Historical Society building destroyed in the 1871 fire
postfire_code_context: A deliberately fire-conscious institutional restart restored archival capacity after the Society's catastrophic 1871 collection and building loss.
notes: Designed as a 40-by-70-foot 'temporary' building but intended as the rear of a future north wing. Contemporary estimate was about $7,000; the Society occupied it October 16, 1877 and removed it in 1892.

address_historical: citywide Chicago fire-alarm network
architect_or_builder: J. P. Barrett (superintendent); municipal fire-alarm staff
structural_system: 174 street boxes; 125 miles aerial wire; 2358 telegraph poles; engine-house control apparatus
postfire_code_context: Directly responsive to the city's post-fire emphasis on detection, communication, and coordinated suppression.
notes: In 1877 the city installed 174 street boxes, connected talking lines to almost all engine houses, added 28 automatic registers, installed door/gas control equipment, built 125 miles of aerial wire including 50 new miles, and moved wires off rooftops onto 2,358 poles.

demolition_cause: western two of five demolished in 1960
address_historical: Erie Street row east of St. Clair Street
postfire_code_context: Masonry rowhouses reflect durable construction in the post-fire North Side.
notes: Five attached rowhouses were built about 1877; the three eastern houses survive, the two western houses were demolished in 1960, and surviving units were converted to commercial use around 1920. Recorded as one grouped complex, not five invented individual identities.

address_historical: Cass Street between Superior and Erie Streets
architect_or_builder: Day & Co. of New York (Kerite cable)
structural_system: two 1955-foot No. 16 copper conductors in one-inch iron pipe with tar insulation
postfire_code_context: The underground cable was a fire-resilience and communications experiment within the rebuilt North Side.
notes: Laid in October 1877 and described by Andreas as Chicago's first regular underground cable, distinct from cables in water tunnels or mains.

address_historical: Fuller Street crossing of the Chicago River
structural_system: combination draw or pivot bridge with swing and turntable
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Fuller Street bridge destroyed by storm
postfire_code_context: Municipal bridge replacement used a movable combination structure suited to the post-fire industrial river.
notes: Completed August 4, 1877; 127 feet long, 16.5-foot roadway, 19.5 feet overall, and $4,210 cost.

address_historical: Harrison Street crossing of the Chicago River
postfire_code_context: Substantial iron infrastructure replaced or extended the pre-fire river-crossing system.
notes: Work began June 22, 1875 but land-condemnation litigation delayed completion until October 23, 1877; 175 feet long, 19-foot roadway, two 4.1-foot sidewalks, 31 feet overall, and $41,848.51 cost.

address_historical: 318-320 Wabash Avenue; northeast corner of Wabash Avenue and Congress Street
address_modern: Northeast corner of S Wabash Ave and E Ida B Wells Dr
postfire_code_context: Substantial masonry hotel construction within the post-fire commercial district.
notes: Chicago Tribune described the hotel as just completed on November 11, 1877. The secondary compilation gives a 1877-1887 lifespan; architect and owner remain unresolved.

canonical_name: Interstate Exposition Building temporary Field & Leiter conversion
address_historical: Lakefront at the foot of Adams Street
architect_or_builder: W. W. Boyington (original 1873 building); temporary fit-out contractor unknown
structural_system: iron and glass exposition structure with temporary partitions counters and shelving
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Interstate Exposition Building of 1873; temporary relocation after Singer Building fire of Nov. 14, 1877
postfire_code_context: Adaptive reuse provided rapid business continuity after a major post-fire-era commercial building fire.
notes: In little over a week, roughly two-thirds of the Exposition Building was partitioned and fitted with shelves and counters; Field & Leiter opened the temporary store November 27, 1877. This row records the conversion, not construction of the 1873 hall.

canonical_name: J. K. Russell & Co. multi-tenant factory
original_use: planing mill plus sash door blind and furniture manufacturing
owner_or_developer: J. K. Russell & Co. and four other manufacturing firms
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Successive J. K. Russell mills destroyed by fires in 1852, 1856, 1860, 1868, and 1869; interim warehouse factory
postfire_code_context: Repeated mill fires made this a long-cycle industrial replacement rather than a direct 1871-fire reconstruction.
notes: Completed early in 1877 and occupied by five firms. Andreas reports about 300 workers in the whole building, including roughly 95 in Russell's factory and planing mill; the address of this specific building was not stated in the passage.

canonical_name: J. W. Reedy Elevator Manufacturing factory rebuild
address_historical: 83-91 Illinois Street
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Reedy factory rebuilt after the 1871 fire and burned again October 14, 1877
postfire_code_context: Rapid industrial reconstruction within the post-fire city; the predecessor was a large brick factory.
notes: Factory burned October 14 and was rebuilt by December 1, 1877. Andreas's compressed business chronology does not supply dimensions or the architect.

address_historical: Northeast corner of West Adams and Throop Streets
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Temporary frame church on the same lot
postfire_code_context: The large brick church replaced a temporary frame edifice and conformed to the post-1874 citywide fire-limit regime.
notes: Construction began in summer 1876 and the church was dedicated January 6, 1877. Reported cost exceeded $45,000 and seating capacity was 800.

address_historical: North Halsted Street crossing of the Chicago River
postfire_code_context: Municipal movable-bridge construction supported the rebuilt city's river traffic and street network.
notes: Begun June 22 and completed October 8, 1877; 140 feet long, 17-foot roadway, 20 feet overall, and $4,190 cost.

address_historical: Northwest corner of Huron and Pine Streets
address_modern: Northwest corner of W Huron St and N Michigan Ave
structural_system: ornate masonry mansion with conservatory and interior theater
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Perry H. Smith pre-fire Pine Street residence destroyed in 1871
postfire_code_context: A high-cost masonry mansion epitomized elite North Side reconstruction after the fire.
notes: A dinner was held in the new mansion November 8, 1877 and a major reception followed January 1, 1878. Later reporting gives $241,000 cost and 1877 completion; the building was demolished in 1918 for boulevard widening.

address_historical: Grand Avenue and North Paulina Street
postfire_code_context: The long-delayed project spanned the 1871 rebuilding labor/material shock and the Panic of 1873; its masonry form fit the post-fire regime.
notes: Secondary research says work begun about 1870/71 finally opened in 1877 without the planned towers and with interior decoration incomplete. A 1916 diocesan souvenir instead calls it erected in 1871, so the completion chronology requires direct newspaper verification.

address_historical: Van Horn and Paulina Streets
postfire_code_context: The frame church lay in the post-1874 citywide fire-limit era; its apparent continued frame use reflects enlargement of existing fabric rather than a new wooden building.
notes: Existing frame church enlarged in 1877 from roughly 300 to 650 seats.

canonical_name: Woman's Hospital Medical College first building
address_historical: Lincoln Street opposite Cook County Hospital
postfire_code_context: The purpose-built or acquired medical-school facility formed part of the post-fire institutional district around Cook County Hospital.
notes: An 1893 account says the first building was erected in 1877; Encyclopedia of Chicago says faculty financed purchase of a school building that year. Later building dimensions were 100 by 65 feet, but may include the 1889 addition. Kept as one review-flagged event pending deed and permit research.

canonical_name: Fullerton Avenue Bridge contract and construction
address_historical: Fullerton Avenue at the north city limits; joint City of Chicago-Town of Lake View crossing
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and Town of Lake View
postfire_code_context: Joint-jurisdiction infrastructure extended the street network at Chicago's 1877 northern boundary.
notes: Contract awarded October 1, 1877 and bridge completed January 19, 1878; 125 feet long, 17.4-foot roadway, 20 feet overall. Chicago paid two-thirds of the reported $2,970.50 cost share wording, which should be checked in the printed scan.

address_historical: North Avenue crossing of the Chicago River
postfire_code_context: Municipal movable-bridge construction supported the rebuilt city's river traffic and street network.
notes: Begun August 28, 1877 and completed in January 1878; 150 feet long, 17-foot roadway, 4-foot sidewalk, 29 feet overall, and $7,149 cost.

canonical_name: United States Government Building cut-stone phase
address_historical: Block bounded by Adams, Clark, Jackson, and Dearborn Streets

architect_or_builder: Alfred B. Mullett; James G. Gill; Edward J. Burling (construction supervision); John Angus (stone setting)
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Federal custom house and post office destroyed in the 1871 fire
postfire_code_context: The monumental fireproof federal replacement was a direct institutional response to the 1871 destruction.
notes: Andreas states John Angus had charge of setting cut-stone work beginning in 1877; the OCR-obscured ending year is unresolved. The building was occupied by 1879 and completed in 1880; recorded here only as a distinct 1877 phase.

address_historical: Noble and Potomac Streets
structural_system: yellow brick with limestone accents; Renaissance Revival
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Wooden 1869 St. Stanislaus Kostka church
postfire_code_context: Substantial masonry expansion followed explosive parish growth during Chicago's post-fire rebuilding era.
notes: Cornerstone laid July 1, 1877; completed in 1881. Parish account gives interior dimensions of 200 by 80 feet and seating for 1,500. Twin towers were completed in 1892; the south tower was destroyed by fire in 1964.

address_historical: Original Court House Square; west half of block bounded by Clark, Randolph, LaSalle, and Washington Streets
architect_or_builder: J. J. Egan (uniform exterior); L. D. Cleveland (city interior and construction supervision); John Shackley (excavation); Mortimer & Tapper (sub-basement)
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Court House and City Hall destroyed in 1871; temporary Rookery City Hall occupied 1872-1885
postfire_code_context: Permanent fire-conscious civic rebuilding on the original courthouse square; exterior coordination with the county emphasized a unified monumental masonry complex.
notes: The City Council ordinance of September 3, 1877 authorized immediate foundation work. Excavation was contracted for $1,483 and the sub-basement for $57,909; later superstructure contracts were awarded in 1878.

address_historical: Corner of Wabash Avenue and Monroe Street
postfire_code_context: Commercial masonry infill continued within the fire-limits district.
notes: Chicago Tribune reported work progressing rapidly on September 16, 1877. Completion, dimensions, architect, and exact corner remain unresolved; retained as a phase record rather than an assumed completion.

address_historical: Wabash Avenue between Monroe and Madison Streets
postfire_code_context: Commercial masonry infill continued within the fire-limits district.
notes: Two stores were reported nearly completed September 16, 1877. They remain grouped because the contemporary notice gives no separate names or addresses; no anonymous unit-level rows were fabricated.

canonical_name: Woman's Christian Association boarding house opening
address_historical: 1514-1516 Wabash Avenue
original_use: affordable Christian boarding house for working and studying women
postfire_code_context: No construction claim is made; the record captures institutional reuse/occupancy of urban building stock.
notes: Boarding house opened May 22, 1877 for seamstresses, teachers, students, clerks, and compositors. Source does not state that a new building was erected or what alterations occurred, so this is explicitly an occupancy-only review record.

address_historical: 83 S. Halsted Street, near Madison Street
owner_or_developer: William B. Clapp (owner); J. K. Emmett (lessee)
structural_system: brick side and rear walls; cut-stone three-story front
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Academy of Music I, destroyed by fire February 4-5, 1878
postfire_code_context: A rapid but substantially enlarged masonry reconstruction followed a theater fire within the post-fire city.
notes: Work was planned to begin in early May; the 75-by-120-foot, approximately $50,000 theater opened September 16, 1878. It burned October 12, 1880.

address_historical: 155-157 Dearborn Street; just north of the Chicago Journal office
owner_or_developer: B. R. Chambers; upper floors rented to Blakely & Brown
postfire_code_context: A five-story purpose-adapted commercial building supported the post-fire printing industry.
notes: The architect's project list identifies the 1878 Chambers block and its intended Blakely & Brown tenancy. Andreas independently says Blakely & Brown moved in 1878 to a five-story building they 'had erected' at 155-157 Dearborn; ownership/development wording needs lease research.

address_historical: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex near South Park Avenue and Twenty-third Street
original_use: brewery horses, vehicles, and service functions
postfire_code_context: A permanent brick service building expanded the logistics capacity of a large brewery complex.
notes: Andreas explicitly dates the large brick barn to 1878. Its footprint, stories, architect, cost, and exact side of the avenue require Sanborn or Robinson map reconciliation.

canonical_name: Bemis & McAvoy Brewery East-Side Icehouse of 1878
address_historical: East side of South Park Avenue near Twenty-third Street
structural_system: substantial industrial construction; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: Specialized industrial construction expanded a major post-fire brewery complex.
notes: Andreas states that two additional icehouses were erected on the east side of South Park Avenue in 1878 and 1879, implying one annual addition but not labeling the individual buildings. Entity matching to insurance maps is required.

address_historical: 48-54 Dearborn Street
original_use: retail, classrooms, library, reading room, and gymnasium
structural_system: pressed brick with brownstone facings and trim
postfire_code_context: A purpose-built masonry educational and commercial block marked permanent cultural reconstruction.
notes: Erected for the Athenaeum's special accommodation; the institution moved in during spring 1878. Andreas gives a 90-by-80-foot plan and a two-story-height gymnasium occupying the upper floors; contemporary project citations place design/construction in 1877.

canonical_name: Chicago Fire Patrol Headquarters at 176 Monroe Street
address_historical: 176 Monroe Street
architect_or_builder: L. Z. Leiter (building erection); Chicago Fire Patrol members (interior finishing and arrangements)
owner_or_developer: L. Z. Leiter; Chicago Board of Underwriters/Chicago Fire Patrol
structural_system: masonry building; detailed material not stated
postfire_code_context: A permanent fire-salvage headquarters was a direct institutional response to Chicago's repeated conflagrations.
notes: Captain Bullwinkle's company formally opened and occupied the headquarters February 16, 1878. Andreas distinguishes Leiter's building work from the patrol members' interior finishing.

canonical_name: Church of the Immaculate Conception Priest's Residence
address_historical: Immediately south of the Church of the Immaculate Conception on the Near North Side
structural_system: likely brick masonry; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: Parish residential construction supplemented the brick church rebuilt in 1874 around the surviving pre-fire basement.
notes: Andreas gives two conflicting costs—about $7,000 in the parish narrative and about $5,000 in Rev. P. T. Butler's biography. Precise historic street address remains unresolved.

address_historical: Northeast corner of Dearborn and Monroe Streets
original_use: heavy printing, paper company, and commercial tenants
owner_or_developer: Daniel F. Crilly; leased ground from Chicago Board of Education
postfire_code_context: Heavy-load commercial construction on a fire-cleared corner advanced the rebuilt printing district.
notes: Crilly leased the corner in 1878 and put up a five-story building for J. M. W. Jones Printing Company; Indianapolis Paper Company occupied the north part. Two stories were added in 1888. Later summaries that call it seven stories in 1878 conflate the phases.

address_historical: Eighteenth Street at Lumber Street over the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne & Chicago and Chicago, Alton & St. Louis railway tracks
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago; Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne & Chicago Railway Company contribution
structural_system: wrought-iron superstructure with two truss-girder spans
postfire_code_context: A permanent iron viaduct reduced street-rail conflicts in the rapidly rebuilding industrial city.
notes: Work began August 1 or 3, 1878; completed December 18, 1878; put in operation February 7, 1879. Andreas contains conflicting total and substructure costs ($20,409.16/$15,215.16 versus $17,196.56/$10,403.43); the wrought-iron superstructure is separately stated as $11,194.

canonical_name: First Regiment Illinois National Guard Armory I
address_historical: Jackson Street between Michigan and Wabash Avenues; later 22-26 Jackson Street
original_use: military drill, company rooms, exhibitions, concerts, and rifle practice
owner_or_developer: Union Mutual Life Insurance Company of Maine; leased to First Regiment Illinois National Guard
structural_system: rough-stone Gothic front; iron posts; timber roof; double floors with mortar sound-deadening
postfire_code_context: Purpose-built masonry and iron institutional construction reflected permanent civic investment after the 1877 labor riots.
notes: Contemporary report said completion was expected September 1, perhaps ten days later. Reported construction cost was $22,000 against an $18,000 limit, plus about $1,400 for the rear boiler and engine room.

canonical_name: Fullerton Avenue Pile Bridge reported as rebuilt
address_historical: Fullerton Avenue
postfire_code_context: The source preserves a bridge-rebuild claim, but entity resolution is necessary before treating it as a separate 1878 structure.
notes: Andreas says a Fullerton Avenue bridge was rebuilt in 1878 at 225 by 20 feet for $1,490. Those dimensions and cost exactly match a Fullerton pile bridge reported in the 1874-75 Board of Public Works year, while a separate 125-foot pivot bridge was completed January 19, 1878. This row preserves the conflict and must not be double-counted in resolved statistics.

address_historical: Fullerton Avenue at the north city limits; joint City of Chicago-Town of Lake View crossing
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and Town of Lake View
postfire_code_context: Joint-jurisdiction infrastructure extended the street network at Chicago's northern boundary.
notes: Contract awarded October 1, 1877; completed January 19, 1878; 125 feet long, 17.4-foot roadway, 20 feet overall. Andreas says Chicago's two-thirds cost was $2,970.50, wording that merits scan verification.

address_historical: Rear of the Hamlin Brothers property on the former Bryan Hall and Hooley's Opera House site
owner_or_developer: "Hamlin Brothers; property passed to William C. Reynolds about 1878"
structural_system: reconstructed existing hall and adjoining fabric
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Foley's Billiard Hall, later garden and vaudeville theater
postfire_code_context: Repeated adaptive reuse converted post-fire commercial entertainment fabric into a regular theater.
notes: The former 1873 billiard hall/garden/vaudeville was reconstructed as a regular theater and opened in September 1878 as Hamlin's Theater. It was reconstructed again in 1880 as the Grand Opera House.

address_historical: Northwest corner of Dearborn and Monroe Streets
structural_system: reused masonry walls with reconstructed interior and galleries
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: New Adelphi Theater opened January 11, 1875 in the old post-office walls
postfire_code_context: A major reconstruction reused strong surviving masonry while upgrading a prominent theater.
notes: Entirely reconstructed and redecorated in July-August 1878; reopened August 4. Work included plate glass, new scenery and curtain, frescoing, upholstery, and carpets, at a reported minimum cost of $8,500.

address_historical: Third Avenue at Taylor Street
postfire_code_context: Purpose-built flats document the diversification and densification of post-fire housing.
notes: Listed among Cyrus P. Thomas's 1878 works with a May 19, 1878 Chicago Tribune citation. Exact unit count, dimensions, material, cost, and fate need the original notice and permit ledger.

canonical_name: Misses Grant's Seminary for Young Ladies
address_historical: 839 N. Dearborn Street / 27-31 W. Chestnut Street
address_modern: 839 N Dearborn St / 27-31 W Chestnut St
structural_system: red brick with gray limestone trim and brown ashlar ground level
postfire_code_context: A substantial masonry educational building represented permanent Near North Side rebuilding.
notes: The National Register nomination identifies the 1878 contributing building and describes its massive corner form, turret, gable, dormers, and contrasting masonry. Andreas notes that the school moved into its new building in November 1878.

address_historical: Rear of 827-833 N. Dearborn Street
postfire_code_context: Documented service buildings preserve the complete residential property system rather than only street-facing houses.
notes: The National Register nomination separately counts the 1878 barns as contributing buildings but does not attribute an architect in its resource table. Count and materials require inventory-sheet review.

address_historical: 827-833 N. Dearborn Street
postfire_code_context: A coordinated masonry rowhouse group contributed to permanent Near North Side residential reconstruction.
notes: The National Register nomination records four 1878 contributing rowhouses. Unit-level owners, exact completion dates, and later alterations need deed and permit research.

address_historical: North Avenue crossing of the Chicago River
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Earlier crossing at North Avenue
postfire_code_context: Municipal movable-bridge construction supported the rebuilt city's river traffic and street network.
notes: Begun August 28, 1877 and completed in January 1878; 150 feet long, with 17-foot roadway, 4-foot sidewalk, 29-foot overall width, and $7,149 cost.

address_historical: Northeast corner of Market and Hill Streets
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Temporary post-fire frame St. Joseph's church; pre-fire church destroyed in 1871
postfire_code_context: Permanent brick rebuilding followed the parish's temporary post-fire frame structure.
notes: Cornerstone laid in October 1876; dedicated October 6, 1878; reported cost about $40,000.

address_historical: Dearborn Avenue north of Schiller Street
postfire_code_context: The project illustrates documented elite residential growth outside the central fire district.
notes: Listed among Cyrus P. Thomas's 1878 works with a contemporary Chicago Tribune citation; dimensions, material, exact address, and fate require the newspaper and permit record.

canonical_name: Third Presbyterian Church on Ashland Avenue
address_historical: Ashland Avenue at or near Ogden Avenue
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Third Presbyterian Church at Washington and Carpenter Streets, sold in 1877
postfire_code_context: A large permanent West Side church replaced the congregation's earlier property after post-fire neighborhood movement.
notes: The new Ashland Avenue edifice was occupied in May 1878 and seated 1,900. It burned October 10, 1884 and was rebuilt materially on the old plan for reopening May 24, 1885.

canonical_name: Daniel Wells Commercial and Hotel Block
address_historical: Michigan Avenue at Harrison Street
original_use: stores, commercial space, and corner hotel
postfire_code_context: A substantial mixed-use block extended permanent masonry development along Michigan Avenue.
notes: The architect's project list dates the four-story block 1878-79 and cites Tribune notices of May 19, 1878 and April 6, 1879. The precise start and completion dates remain to be recovered from those notices.

canonical_name: U.S. Government Building and Post Office construction phase
address_historical: Block bounded by Adams, Clark, Jackson, and Dearborn Streets
original_use: post office, custom house, sub-treasury, federal courts, pension and internal revenue offices
architect_or_builder: Alfred B. Mullett (original design); U.S. Treasury Supervising Architect's Office
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Federal post office and custom house destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: Explicitly fireproof federal construction replaced dispersed rented quarters described in 1878 as vulnerable to fire.
notes: The June 10, 1878 Congressional Record documents active work, a $300,000 bill appropriation plus $100,000 deficiency funding, and a proposed acceleration toward 1879 occupancy. The post office occupied part of the basement in April 1879; the entire building was completed about 1880.

canonical_name: Chicago City Hall and Cook County Court House construction phase
address_historical: Original Court House Square; block bounded by Clark, Randolph, LaSalle, and Washington Streets
architect_or_builder: J. J. Egan (uniform exterior); L. D. Cleveland (city interior and construction supervision); Thomlinson & Reed (cut stone); John Angus (masonry); J. P. Sexton (iron)
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and Cook County
structural_system: stone, brick, granite, and iron civic complex
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Court House and City Hall destroyed in 1871; temporary Rookery City Hall occupied 1872-1885
postfire_code_context: Permanent monumental masonry and iron construction on the original civic square embodied long-term post-fire institutional rebuilding.
notes: On April 17, 1878 the city awarded contracts of $477,693 for cut stone, $90,519 for masonry, and $105,302 for iron work. The joint complex was not ready for occupancy until January-February 1885.

canonical_name: House of the Good Shepherd North Wing
address_historical: Corner of North Market and Hill Streets
structural_system: masonry wing; exact material not stated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: House of the Good Shepherd post-fire building erected 1872
postfire_code_context: A permanent institutional addition enlarged the rebuilt post-fire complex.
notes: A summer 1878 bazaar and benefits produced net receipts of $8,695, applied to erecting the north wing. The source does not state an exact completion date, so the annual placement records a materially documented construction expenditure/phase.

address_historical: Lake Michigan shore at Lincoln Park
structural_system: Netherlands-plan brush mattresses laid in three to five feet of water
postfire_code_context: Permanent engineered shore protection replaced temporary expedients and shaped the lakefront land edge.
notes: Andreas states construction commenced in 1878 using the Netherlands plan. Completion date and surviving fabric require park-commission annual reports and georeferencing.

address_historical: Corner of West Van Buren Street and Albany Avenue
original_use: convent, home, instruction, and vocational work
structural_system: brick and stone; iron entrance stairways
postfire_code_context: Substantial masonry institutional construction replaced the order's initial rented quarters at 1266 W. Van Buren.
notes: The sisters established their home in May 1878; construction on a 300-foot-square site began in 1878 and Vicar-General McMullen laid the cornerstone. Andreas still described the convent as unfinished in 1886; adjoining buildings were two and three stories.

address_historical: Eighteenth Street railroad crossing
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and affected railroads
postfire_code_context: Durable iron infrastructure aligned with post-fire material preferences, though grade separation was its primary purpose.
notes: Completed December 18, 1878 and put in operation February 7, 1879. Andreas reports $11,194 cost, two 142-foot truss-girder spans, a 20-foot roadway and six-foot sidewalks. Not counted as 1879 construction.

canonical_name: Field, Leiter & Co. State Street store occupancy
address_historical: Northeast corner State and Washington Streets
owner_or_developer: Singer estate; purchased by Field, Leiter & Co.
structural_system: masonry commercial building; exact 1879 fit-out materials not established
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Singer Building destroyed by fire and replaced in 1878
postfire_code_context: The underlying replacement belonged to post-fire masonry commercial rebuilding; this row does not claim new 1879 construction.
notes: Field and Leiter purchased the 1878 replacement building on February 28, 1879, secured surrender of Carson Pirie's lease, fitted it for their business, and received customers there by April. Retained as a property and occupancy phase only.

canonical_name: Academy of the Sacred Heart chapel
address_historical: Adjoining the Academy of the Sacred Heart
address_modern: West Side academy complex; exact parcel unresolved
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Academy of the Sacred Heart
postfire_code_context: Post-fire institutional construction; exact material and code compliance are not documented in the located narrative.
notes: Andreas reports that a chapel was built adjoining the academy in 1879. No separate street number, architect, dimensions or material were located, so the row remains a named complex phase rather than a guessed standalone footprint.

address_historical: Armour Street
structural_system: brick masonry; heating recorded as steam by Andreas but coal stoves by CPS history
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings; the heating conflict remains unresolved.

CPS says it opened during the 1878-79 academic year and initially used coal stoves and gas; this may indicate a start/opening/completion sequence or a table error.

address_historical: Immediately south of the Bemis & McAvoy brewhouse
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex
postfire_code_context: Brick office construction complied with the post-1874 restriction on new wood buildings.
notes: Erected in 1879. Andreas describes a substantial two-story brick office south of the brewhouse with the main business office and billiard rooms.

address_historical: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex, east side
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex
postfire_code_context: An industrial outbuilding erected after the citywide wood-building restriction; material and permit compliance remain unverified.
notes: Andreas says two east-side ice houses were erected in 1878 and 1879. This row assigns one phase to 1879 but does not infer dimensions, material or a precise address; component identity needs brewery and permit records.

address_historical: Southeast corner State and Randolph Streets
original_use: music hall, public assembly, offices and stores
owner_or_developer: Central Music Hall stock company; George B. Carpenter promoter; Levi Z. Leiter president
structural_system: fireproof masonry commercial and assembly building with gray cut-stone exterior
postfire_code_context: The building's fireproof construction, abundant exits, ventilation and public-assembly safeguards responded directly to post-fire and theater-safety concerns.
notes: Erected and opened in 1879. Later descriptions give a 125-by-150-foot footprint, six stories plus basement, two elevators, stores and offices; seating is variously reported around 1,800 to 2,000. The December 1879 inspection emphasizes acoustics, rapid air exchange, multiple exits and fire-safety planning.

canonical_name: Chicago fire-alarm system Stock Yards extension
address_historical: Stock Yards district, Town of Lake
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago; Town of Lake stations
structural_system: aerial telegraph wire, alarm stations and Tooker keyless-door box retrofits
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Chicago municipal fire-alarm system
postfire_code_context: The extension increased fire-detection coverage and retrofitted 72 existing boxes with keyless doors, a direct post-fire life-safety investment.
notes: Andreas reports extension of aerial lines to the Stock Yards district in the Town of Lake, establishment of fire-alarm stations, and Tooker keyless-door attachments on 72 existing boxes. It is a network event extending beyond the 1879 municipal boundary, not one building.

address_historical: 135 Rush Street at Erie Street; southeast corner Rush and Huron/Erie block
owner_or_developer: Cyrus H. and Nettie Fowler McCormick
structural_system: Lake Superior sandstone masonry; German Renaissance residence; interior structural system not fully documented
postfire_code_context: The masonry mansion was erected after the 1874 citywide restriction on new wood construction.
notes: The residence was four years in construction, beginning in 1875 and occupied in 1879; a major social dedication followed in May 1880. Contemporary description records three principal stories, brown sandstone, a concert hall and advanced electrical apparatus.

canonical_name: Farwell Hall YMCA gymnasium and bath addition
address_historical: Farwell Hall, downtown Chicago; exact 1879 street number unresolved
owner_or_developer: Young Men's Christian Association of Chicago
structural_system: material and structural system not stated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Farwell Hall YMCA
postfire_code_context: A public-health and recreation addition after the fire; material and fire-code details require YMCA property records.
notes: YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago's institutional chronology states that a gymnasium and bath were added to Farwell Hall in 1879. Exact dimensions, architect, materials and address remain unresolved.

address_historical: Behind Holy Family Church
address_modern: Holy Family Church complex near 1080 W Roosevelt Rd
original_use: Catholic sodality meetings, reading room and libraries
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Holy Family Church complex
postfire_code_context: A large institutional addition in the post-fire city; material and exact fireproofing require parish or permit records.
notes: Erected behind the church in 1879 at a reported cost of $40,000. Andreas describes meeting rooms and halls, a reading room, and two libraries totaling approximately 3,000 volumes.

canonical_name: Kedzie Avenue bridge over the Illinois and Michigan Canal
address_historical: Kedzie Avenue over the Illinois and Michigan Canal
address_modern: Kedzie Avenue near the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal corridor
owner_or_developer: Town of Cicero with shared public expense
postfire_code_context: Wrought iron provided a durable noncombustible crossing; this site lay in adjacent Cicero rather than within the 1879 city boundary.
notes: Completed March 1, 1879. Retained as metropolitan infrastructure tied to Chicago circulation, but flagged because the contemporary jurisdiction was the Town of Cicero.

address_historical: South end of LaSalle Street tunnel
address_modern: LaSalle Street at the Chicago River
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: LaSalle Street tunnel
postfire_code_context: A public-safety access improvement to major post-fire municipal infrastructure; material and ordinance details are not stated.
notes: Andreas reports that a footbridge was placed over the south end of the LaSalle Street tunnel in January 1879. Exact span, material and removal date remain unknown.

address_historical: Southeast corner Randolph Street and Wabash Avenue; 64-66 Wabash Avenue
postfire_code_context: A tall masonry-and-metal commercial block reflects the post-fire move toward durable loft construction.
notes: A later guide reports erection in 1879, 200 feet on Randolph by 40 feet on Wabash, five stories, 85 feet high and two freight elevators. The architect and the exact sequence of later height changes and demolition remain unresolved.

address_historical: Northwest corner Fifth Avenue and Monroe Street; later 200-208 W Monroe Street
address_modern: Northwest corner Wells Street and West Monroe Street
original_use: wholesale clothing store and loft building
structural_system: load-bearing masonry exterior and party walls; cast-iron interior columns/pilasters; timber girders and wood joists; iron, Lemont stone and pressed-brick facade
postfire_code_context: Post-fire commercial construction emphasized masonry and iron, broad daylight openings, heavy floor capacity and fire-prevention equipment.
notes: The 1879 initial building had five stories plus basement; two stories were added in 1888. HABS identifies cast-iron members continuing from foundation to roof as an important step toward skeletal framing, but the building was not a complete metal skeleton. A contemporary account gives approximately 82 ft 10 in by 102 ft 6 in and an estimated $125,000 cost.

address_historical: Lock Street crossing
address_modern: Near present Chicago River and Lock Street alignment
owner_or_developer: Illinois and Michigan Canal Commissioners; State of Illinois
postfire_code_context: The wooden construction was an explicit exception or jurisdictional edge case relative to Chicago's 1874 citywide prohibition on new wood buildings; legal context requires review.
notes: Built in 1879 by the Canal Commissioners at state expense. The exact waterway, city-boundary status, dimensions and later history require engineering and map confirmation.

address_historical: Southwest corner Wood and Congress Streets
address_modern: Cook County medical-campus vicinity near W Harrison St and S Wood St
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Andreas's visually checked 1879 table records 107.5 by 84 feet, three stories, steam heat, 945 sittings and $37,000 including heating and furniture. A later guide independently places the 1879 school at Wood and Congress but gives 800 capacity and $45,000 cost; Andreas controls the annual values pending Board proceedings.

address_historical: Dashiel Street and Thirty-seventh Street; later Union Avenue and 37th Street
owner_or_developer: Nativity of Our Lord Catholic parish
structural_system: masonry Romanesque-Gothic church; detailed materials not stated
postfire_code_context: Masonry church construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Foundation work began in 1876, the cornerstone was laid October 28, 1876, and the church was completed and dedicated September 1, 1879. Historical street-name/address reconciliation and the survival of specific 1879 fabric need architectural survey.

address_historical: 66-72 West Randolph Street with former Clark Street entrance
address_modern: Randolph Street theater district near Clark Street
structural_system: pre-existing masonry theater; exterior and interior thoroughly renovated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Metropolitan Theatre
postfire_code_context: The refit of an existing post-fire assembly building should be evaluated against contemporary theater egress and fire-safety requirements.
notes: A Chicago Tribune account dated August 30, 1879 describes thorough exterior and interior renovation and reopening as the Olympic. This is an adaptive-reuse phase, not a new 1879 building.

address_historical: Wabash Avenue at Thirty-sixth Place
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Andreas's visually checked table records erection in 1879, 70 by 84 feet, three stories, steam heat, 770 sittings and $29,500 total including heating and furniture. A later addition is reported for 1886; the surviving fabric and exact original footprint require Board and fire-insurance-map review.

address_historical: Thirty-sixth Street and Vincennes Avenue
structural_system: masonry church; exact system not independently verified
postfire_code_context: A church dated to 1879 would fall under the post-1874 citywide wood-building prohibition, but material and permit confirmation remain required.
notes: WBEZ reports the church was built in 1879; WTTW corroborates the 3600 South Vincennes identity and later Ida B. Wells Homes context. Primary church, permit or contemporary newspaper confirmation is still needed.

canonical_name: St. Stephen German Evangelical Lutheran Church repair and refit
address_historical: Northwest corner Wentworth Avenue and Twenty-fifth Street
address_modern: Approx. W 25th St and S Wentworth Ave
owner_or_developer: St. Stephen German Evangelical Lutheran congregation
structural_system: pre-existing frame church on brick basement; repaired and refitted
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Pre-existing church building acquired September 1, 1879
postfire_code_context: The retained frame superstructure was pre-existing; the 1879 work was repair and refit rather than prohibited new frame construction.
notes: The congregation organized May 1, purchased the property September 1 for a reported $10,475, thoroughly repaired and refitted the approximately 1,000-seat church, installed an organ reported at $3,000, and dedicated it in fall 1879.

canonical_name: United States Government Building west-basement post-office phase
address_historical: Block bounded by Adams, Clark, Jackson and Dearborn Streets
address_modern: Kluczynski Federal Building and Federal Center site
original_use: post office, custom house and federal offices
architect_or_builder: Alfred B. Mullett; construction administration by federal successors
structural_system: masonry federal building with iron structural and fireproofing systems; phase details require federal specifications
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: 1859 Custom House and Post Office destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: Long-running federal masonry construction embodied post-fire fire-resistance goals; exact assemblies should be verified from federal drawings.
notes: The west half of the basement was finished and turned over for temporary post-office quarters in April 1879. Final building completion was in 1880, so this is not a 1879 whole-building completion despite simplified later references to an 1879 federal building.

canonical_name: Samuel M. Nickerson House construction start
address_historical: 40 Erie Street
structural_system: fire-resistant masonry residence with extensive stone, tile and metal; detailed assemblies documented by HABS
postfire_code_context: The project was explicitly conceived as a fireproof residence in post-fire Chicago.
notes: Commissioned in 1879 and completed in 1883 at a reported cost of about $450,000. Included for the documented 1879 project start, not counted as a 1879 completion.

canonical_name: C. P. Kimball & Co. carriage building opening
address_historical: Chicago; exact 1879 address unresolved
structural_system: five-floor industrial building; material not stated
postfire_code_context: A multi-story industrial occupancy in the post-fire city; the building's material and permit history are not identified.
notes: Andreas says the company opened its building in 1879 and describes the whole building as 40 by 160 feet with five floors. A larger Wabash-and-Harrison facility described elsewhere may be later, so that address is not assigned here. Not counted as verified new construction.
